title: The Mughal Empire: Polity and Administration

cards.b: The Mughals ruled most of India for about 180 years at their peak. Administration (mansabdari, revenue) and culture are tested every year.

Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527), Afghans at Ghaghra (1529). Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), returned in 1555. Sher Shah Suri (1540 to 45): Grand Trunk Road, rupiya, dam, a revenue system based on measurement, and sarais. Humayun’s regaining of Delhi in 1555.

Second Battle of Panipat (1556) with Bairam Khan. Conquests: Malwa, Gondwana, Chittor (1568), Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir, Kandahar, Khandesh. Religious policy: abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564); Ibadat Khana (1575); mahzar (1579); Din-i-Ilahi (1582); sulh-i-kul (peace with all). Court: Abul Fazl, Faizi, Todar Mal, Birbal, Tansen, Man Singh. Rajput alliance.

Mansab = rank. Two numbers: zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (cavalry to be kept). Ranks from 10 to 10,000 (princes higher). Paid by jagirs (revenue assignments) or cash; dagh and chehra continued. Transferable and non-hereditary. Under Shah Jahan, the month scale (masik) and sihbandi. The jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb (shortage of jagirs) is linked by Satish Chandra to the decline.

Todar Mal’s zabt (Akbar’s Dahsala, 1580): measured land, average prices and yields of ten years, revenue in cash (about one-third of produce). Other systems: batai, kankut, nasaq. Crops: wheat, rice, cotton, indigo, sugarcane; new: tobacco, maize, chillies. Trade with Europeans brought silver. Cities: Agra, Lahore, Surat. Craft: cotton textiles of Bengal and Gujarat. The zamindars were intermediaries.

Emperor (Padshah), Wakil, Diwan-i-Kul (finance), Mir Bakhshi (army), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious grants), Mir Saman (household), Qazi-ul-Quzat (justice). 12 subas by Akbar, later more; Subadar, Diwan, Bakhshi, Faujdar, Kotwal. Sarkars and parganas; Amil and qanungo. A centralised system with checks.

Jahangir (1605 to 27): chain of justice, Nur Jahan’s role, painting; Sir Thomas Roe’s embassy (1615). Shah Jahan (1628 to 58): Taj Mahal, new city Shahjahanabad; war of succession (1657 to 58). Aurangzeb (1658 to 1707): reimposed jizya (1679), temple controversies, Deccan campaigns (Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687), revolts of Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (Guru Tegh Bahadur’s execution 1675), Marathas, Rajputs; the Deccan ulcer.

cards.h: Why did the Mughal Empire decline?
cards.b: Irfan Habib (Agrarian System of Mughal India) stresses an agrarian crisis from heavy revenue demands. Satish Chandra points to the jagirdari crisis. M. Athar Ali emphasises the growth of the nobility. Others (Jadunath Sarkar) blamed Aurangzeb’s religious policy; modern scholars (Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly, Chetan Singh) point to regional powers rising and the shift of power to provinces. Balanced answers use several causes.

The Mughal revenue records (Ain-i-Akbari), the idea of an empire-wide administration and the language Urdu (Hindustani) are living legacies. The Grand Trunk Road survives as NH 1 and NH 2. Debates about historical figures in textbooks and place names make the Mughals a political subject. The Red Fort is the site of Independence Day.
